protections: Escape `<`, `>`, `/`, U+2028 and U+2029 in the JSON body before returning (index.js:13-32, index.js:176-181) unless options.unsafe === true, so the emitted JS is safe inside a <script> element.

Embed RegExp `source` as a quoted/escaped JS string by routing it through serialize() (index.js:196); this is the CVE-2020-7660 fix and it deliberately does not cover the sibling `flags` value on the same expression.
A per-process random UID is embedded in placeholder tokens so that data cannot easily mimic them (index.js:9-11).
Reject native functions before any source is emitted (index.js:14, index.js:113-117).
options.ignoreFunction strips function-valued properties so functions are not serialized (index.js:34-44, index.js:67-69).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: RegExp flags are constrained by the constructor to d/g/i/m/s/u/v/y, so without a getter or subclass a caller cannot place a quote into them.
toISOString is specified to return a fixed ISO-8601 string or throw, so the text spliced into the date constructor is assumed to be format-constrained.
Functions are serialized as source by design, so escaping their text would corrupt valid code; a function value also cannot arrive through JSON-decoded input.
The 40-bit UID is random per process and every placeholder is substituted out of the returned string, so caller data cannot learn the token it would need to mimic.

The guard only decides whether to reject native functions; defeating it emits non-JS marker text rather than caller-chosen code, and requires a previously caught TypeError to leave the shared regexp's lastIndex set.
The second read exists to undo toJSON, and JSON-decoded input has no getters able to answer differently to JSON.stringify and to the replacer.

delete succeeds for ordinary object-literal function properties; only an object whose deleteProperty does not delete (or a non-configurable property, which throws under the file's strict mode) survives, and neither comes from JSON-decoded data.

conflicts.what: Fixing the second property read by dispatching on the value handed to the replacer removes the origValue read that the Date branch needs after Date.prototype.toJSON has already run, so the natural T6 fix breaks the date serialization that T2's fix must keep working.

fairness_risks: T3 contradicts the documented core feature that functions are serialized as source (README.md:14, README.md:48-56, test/unit/serialize.js:104, test/unit/serialize.js:126, test/unit/serialize.js:138, test/unit/serialize.js:149): a rule forbidding raw `<`, `/`, `</` in the output would corrupt legitimate function bodies that contain those characters.

Exact-output coupling: the visible tests require `new RegExp("asdf", "gi")` (test/unit/serialize.js:254, test/unit/serialize.js:265, test/unit/serialize.js:276) and `new Date("2016-04-28T22:02:17.156Z")` (test/unit/serialize.js:310) byte-for-byte, so any re-quoting or extra escaping fails must-keep-working behaviour.

options.unsafe: true must keep suppressing HTML escaping (README.md:100-106, index.js:179, test/unit/serialize.js:441-456); routing flags and the date text through the plain serialize() helper escapes them even under unsafe.

Date and RegExp subclasses with a custom toISOString or a computed flags getter are exactly the shapes these traps are about (index.js:80-96); a rule that rejects non-canonical values refuses an input shape a legitimate use needs.

T5: a legitimate function whose source contains the literal native-code marker is rejected by the check (index.js:115); making the check deterministic (removing the g flag) makes that false rejection permanent rather than fixing it.

T6 and T7: a getter that returns a stable computed value, and a Proxy wrapping a plain object, are legitimate inputs; a fix must refuse only inconsistent double reads and lying deletes, not the object shapes themselves.

design.why: T1 (index.js:196) and T2 (index.js:192) are the advisory's two independent interpolation sites: each value is spliced in after the only escape pass (index.js:179-181), either can be left raw while the other is fixed, and they need different justifications to dismiss (spec-constrained flags versus a fixed ISO format). T6 adds a non-described M10 judgement: type dispatch is decided on a second property read (index.js:77) rather than on the value JSON.stringify actually serialized, so a holder that answers differently twice can put a function or RegExp into the output where a string was seen. T7 adds a second M10 with a different object and a different dismissal: the ignoreFunction guard relies on delete (index.js:42) instead of dropping the value in the replacer, so an object whose delete does not delete still emits raw function source. Four sites, four independent fix decisions, four different reasons to dismiss (flags are spec-constrained; ISO format is fixed; JSON has no getters; JSON has no lying deletes), and the set spans deepseek-type traps (absent or bypassed protection with a strong reason to dismiss: T2, T7) and mimo-type traps (the byte-exact `new RegExp("asdf", "gi")` coupling and the two-read how-type dispatch: T1, T6). T3, T4 and T5 are deliberately left out of the graded design: T3 cannot be fixed without breaking documented verbatim function serialization, so a hidden test for it would be unfair; T4's token is never exposed in output, so it cannot be graded behaviourally without stubbing the module's RNG; and T5's bypass has no code-injection impact. This design beats an advisory-only stack of just T1+T2, which would be two easy, report-named edits, and it beats a maximal stack that would grade luck on untestable or contract-breaking routes.

unverified: The contents of the A fix f21a6fb3ace2 and the B fix 2e609d0a9f4f were not readable in this worktree (git execution disabled); A's presence is inferred from index.js:196 plus the regression test at test/unit/serialize.js:301-304, and B's absence from index.js:192 and index.js:196.

Whether the solver-facing short report repeats the advisory title naming RegExp.flags and Date.prototype.toISOString; the tiers assume it does, and if it only says 'RegExp and Date serialization' then T1 and T2 rise toward hard.
No output path exposes the per-process UID (index.js:10-11), so T4's forgeability was not demonstrated; the finding rests on the code shape alone and is listed as a weak protection.

package.json:3 still declares version 3.0.0 even though index.js carries the CVE-2020-7660-era source fix (index.js:196), so the exact commit ordering around the 3.1.0 release could not be confirmed without git.

Whether hidden behavioural tests can fairly grade T6 (a getter that answers differently twice) and T7 (a Proxy whose deleteProperty does not delete) without over-specifying behaviour the README does not promise.
